title: cold-to-warm-transition-race-conditions-log
body:
Short summary:
Observed repeated capacity thrash on the dedicated GPU pool during load bursts. Symptoms: large number of warmup failures, brief overscale followed by rapid downscale and request queuing. Pattern looks like race between warm-instance registration and autoscaler decisions (scale-up triggers before instance reaches full readiness).

Timeline (high level):
- 2025-02-11 09:14 PST: Spike in customer traffic (canary tests) -> autoscaler triggered +6.
- 2025-02-11 09:16 PST: New instances started but kube pods are in CrashLoopBackOff / OOM on init container (kv-cache warm stage).
- 2025-02-11 09:18 PST: Autoscaler sees high CPU/queued requests -> another +4 decision.
- 2025-02-11 09:22 PST: Several preemptible hosts reclaimed, resulting in pod restarts.
- 2025-02-11 09:25 PST: Scale-down hunts: nodes drained then reprovisioned, thrash for ~12 minutes.

Commands I ran (snippet logs included):
$ kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving -l pool=dedicated-gpu -o wide
NAME                                      READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
dedicated-worker-7b9c6                   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff     4          7m
dedicated-worker-8g2m1                   1/1     Running              0          5m

$ rdctl autoscaler status dedicated-gpu --json
{"desired":12,"current_nodes":7,"pending_nodes":5,"last_scale_event":"2025-02-11T09:18:02Z"}

(Observations: desired > current_nodes because new hosts are provisioned but not yet reporting readiness. pending_nodes persisted for >2m)

Init container / warm logs (from pod describe):
Init: fetch-kv-cache: terminated with exit code 1
Error: failed to fetch KV prefix: rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded

nvidia-smi output on a repro node:
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| NVIDIA-SMI 520.61       Driver Version: 520.61       CUDA Version: 12.1     |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| GPU  Name        Persistence-M| Bus-Id        | Volatile Uncorr. ECC |
| 0   A100-SXM4-40GB  On         | 00000000:00:1E.0 | N/A                   |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Warm initialization (KV cache populate + model mmap/quant load) takes variable time (20s-90s). Autoscaler TTL for pending nodes is too short and controller makes repeated scale decisions because metrics lag (queued requests). That creates "overprovision then reclaim" oscillation.
2) Preemptible instance churn: using preemptible hosts for burst capacity plus warm artifacts on ephemeral disk means restart costs high; preemptions correlate with spike windows.
3) Readiness probe semantics: readiness only checks container liveness, not KV population. Service is marked ready prematurely in control plane but not warm for inference, giving false healthy signals to router -> requests fail, causing more scaling.
4) Pod scheduling fragmentation: strict anti-affinity + GPU resource packing leads to nodes with leftover GPU capacity that cannot host new pods, autoscaler requests more nodes.

Quick wins to test (chronological):
- Extend pending node TTL in autoscaler from 60s -> 180s for dedicated-gpu to avoid reactive downscales.
- Modify readiness probe to require KV cache populated marker file (/var/run/kv_ready). Update init container to touch file only after successful warm fetch.
- Add a pre-warm cache layer in shared NFS (fast check) so repeated warm work is cheap if instance recreated within X mins.
- Swap burst pool from preemptible -> spot-with-graceful-eviction or add fallback to non-preemptible during business hours.

Commands to try next (on staging):
- Increase autoscaler TTL: rdctl autoscaler update dedicated-gpu --pending-ttl 180
- Change readiness: update deployment spec readinessProbe exec: ["/bin/test","-f","/var/run/kv_ready"]
- Force a warm cycle: kubectl exec -n redwood-serving dedicated-worker-7b9c6 -- /opt/redwood/warmup --force

Recent observations after small test run (2025-02-25):
- With TTL=180s, pending_nodes stabilized (desired=8, current=6, pending=2) and no immediate scale down for 4m.
- Readiness change prevented router from routing to unready pods, queue time reduced by ~30%.
- However, total cold-to-ready time remained ~40s median due to heavy mmap time; still need model artifact local caching improvement.

Error snippets to monitor (prometheus alerts to add):
- "kv_fetch_deadline_exceeded" from warmup service
- "pod_ready_but_not_in_router" (custom metric when kube readiness true but router healthcheck fails)
- "node_preempted_count" spike correlated with scale-up windows

Open debugging TODOs: (short actionable list)
- [ ] Reproduce with forced throttled network to simulate cold remote store and measure exact KV fetch time distribution (Maya/Ethan).
- [ ] Prototype mmap-once shared cache (/tmp/model_cache) on instance bootstrap; measure warm delta (Jordan).
- [ ] Evaluate moving warm batch provisioning to Dedicated controller (prevent preemptible use) during high-SLO hours (product/ops).
- [ ] Add a metric: warm_ready_latency_ms (histogram) and emit at the end of init container.

Notes on broader impact:
- End-user latency SLOs suffer only during bursts because requests queue for warm instances; cost spikes as autoscaler overshoots. Solution reduces both latency and unit cost (less wasted churn).

Immediate next steps (this week):
- Patch readiness probe + extend autoscaler TTL in staging (FRI: 2025-03-03).
- Run 4 controlled bursts and gather warm_ready_latency + pending_nodes timelines.
- If improvement >25% in median queue, schedule rollout to canary account (opt-in customers) and monitor.

Raw scratch area / random notes:
- Consider opportunistic background pre-warm during low-traffic windows (02:00-04:00 local) to keep some ephemeral cache hot.
- Check spot termination notices delivery and whether init container can checkpoint partial KV to survive short preemptions.
- Possible follow-up: offload heavy kv-fetch to a sidecar that warms cache independently of serving container lifecycle.

End of scratch log.
